# Results

## Study population

The included study population had a mean age of 66 years (SD = 7.1) and 53% were men. The mean BMI was 27 kg/m² (SD = 4.5) and the majority were current smokers (63%). Glycemic categories were distributed as follows: 734 (53%) NGT, 249 (18%) iIFG, 122 (9%) iIGT, 116 (8%) IFG+IGT and 160 (12%) type 2 diabetes. Regarding body fat distribution, women had higher body fat percentage and SAT than men, while men had higher VAT and VAT/SAT ratio. Participants excluded from the clustering analysis were more likely to have higher BMI, waist circumference, VAT and HbA1c compared to the included participants. Participants excluded from the regression analysis were more likely to have type 2 diabetes, impaired glucose tolerance and had higher BMI compared to the included participants.

## K-means clustering

A three-cluster solution was identified as the most appropriate clustering solution based on statistical criteria, distinct OGTT-profiles and sufficient cluster sizes, with an overall silhouette width of 0.21. While the NbClust package indicated highest support for two and nine clusters, a two-cluster solution collapsed the incretin and glucagon heterogeneity into a single group dominated by differences in glucose and insulin sensitivity, and solutions with more than three clusters produced very small clusters (n = 2) driven by extreme values on glucagon suppression. Cluster characteristics of the three-cluster solution are presented in Table 1. Cluster 1 (n = 459) had the youngest mean age, highest proportion of males and highest physical activity level, while cluster 2 (n = 491) had the highest proportion of women and cluster 3 (n = 431) had the oldest mean age and highest proportion of current smokers. Regarding adiposity, Cluster 3 had the highest BMI, waist circumference, body fat percentage, and VAT in both men and women, while Cluster 2 had the lowest BMI, waist circumference and SAT, and Cluster 1 had the lowest VAT and VAT/SAT ratio. The distribution of glycemic status differed markedly across clusters. Cluster 3 had the highest proportion of type 2 diabetes (33%), IFG+IGT (25%) and iIGT (21%), while the majority of individuals in clusters 1 and 2 had normoglycemia (69% and 78%, respectively). Sex-stratified clustering (supplementary Table S1) produced three broadly similar clusters in both men and women, with consistent within and between-cluster differences similar to the main analysis.

Figure 1 shows characteristics of clustering variables across clusters. The OGTT response patterns underlying these clusters are shown in Figure 2, with mean response curves for glucose, insulin, GLP-1, GIP and glucagon (*Fig. 2A, B, C, D* and *E,* respectively) at all three time points (0, 30 and 120 minutes). Cluster 3 was characterized by the highest FPG and 2hPG, alongside the highest insulin concentrations throughout the OGTT and the lowest insulin sensitivity across clusters. In contrast, cluster 2 had the lowest 2hPG, higher 30-minute insulin than cluster 1 and the highest insulin sensitivity. Cluster 1 had the lowest incretin secretion with substantially lower GLP-1 and GIP secretion than cluster 2. Glucagon response patterns also differed between clusters. Cluster 3 showed impaired early glucagon suppression, whereas cluster 2 had lower glucagon suppression than cluster 1 across all intervals. Despite differences in early and late response patterns, clusters 1 and 3 had similar overall glucagon suppression while cluster 3 had the highest overall glucagon secretion. Detailed OGTT measurements are shown in supplementary Table S2.

## Associations with measures of fat distribution

Estimates from all four outcome models, representing associations between cluster membership and measures of body fat distribution, are shown in Table 2 and reported as mean differences in SD units on the log-scale for VAT, SAT and VAT/SAT ratio and on the original scale for body fat percentage. In the model adjusted for age and sex, cluster 3 had higher VAT, SAT, VAT/SAT ratio and body fat percentage than cluster 2, with the largest differences observed in VAT and body fat percentage (0.68 SD, 95% CI 0.56; 0.81 and 0.63 SD, 95% CI 0.52; 0.73, respectively). Cluster 1 had similar VAT to cluster 2 (-0.03 SD, 95% CI -0.15; 0.09), but higher SAT (0.25 SD, 95% CI 0.12; 0.38), higher body fat percentage (0.15 SD, 95% CI 0.05; 0.25) and lower VAT/SAT ratio (-0.23, 95% CI -0.34; -0.11). Estimates were largely unchanged after further adjustment for smoking and physical activity. No sex-by-cluster interactions were observed for measures of body fat distribution (p \> 0.05), and interaction terms were therefore not included in the main models. Sex-specific associations are illustrated in supplementary Figure S1, and regression models on the original outcome scales can be found in supplementary Table S3.
